etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French immense, from Latin immensus, from in- (“not”) + mensus (“measured”). Compare incommensurable.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter V, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Then everybody once more knelt, and soon the blessing was pronounced. The choir and the clergy trooped out slowly,  […] , down the nave to the western door.  […]  At a seemingly immense distance the surpliced group stopped to say the last prayer.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: The gallant young Indian dandies at home on furlough—immense dandies these—chained and moustached—driving in tearing cabs  […]

quote.citation: 1882, James Thomson (B. V.), Despotism Tempered by Dynamite:
quote.text: The half of Asia is my prison-house,Myriads of convicts lost in its Immense—I look with terror to my crowning day.
